query: For high-entropy alloys intended for harsh corrosive mechanical environments, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion, and why? Propose a controlled comparison that would test the hypothesis, predict how combined degradation and its wear and corrosion components would differ from a matched baseline, define where the prediction should hold or fail, identify supporting prior evidence, and state an observation that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in high‐entropy alloys is governed by a self‐adaptative surface mechanism in which the inherent chemical complexity and lattice distortions promote dynamic grain refinement and/or local amorphization under mechanical stress. This, in turn, facilitates the rapid formation and continual repair of a dense, protective passive oxide layer that mitigates both corrosive attack and mechanical damage.
generation.material_initial_state: A bulk or coating high‐entropy alloy (e.g., a CoCrFeNiMo‐based alloy) produced by conventional solid‐state processing methods that yields a fairly homogeneous microstructure without engineered surface nanostructuring.
generation.intervention: Expose the alloy to a controlled tribocorrosion test that combines sliding wear (to induce surface strain) with immersion in a corrosive medium (e.g., 3.5 wt% NaCl solution). Optionally, compare a pre-conditioned sample (designed to trigger surface nanostructuring) with a matched untreated baseline.
generation.conditions: Tribological testing at room temperature in a 3.5 wt% NaCl aqueous solution using a sliding (or reciprocating) wear test under constant load and controlled speed for a prolonged period (hours), with concurrent electrochemical monitoring.
generation.structural_mediator: An adaptive ultra-nanocrystalline (or partially amorphized) surface layer that is enriched in corrosion-resistant oxide species.
generation.mechanism: Under mechanical loading, high local strains induce dynamic grain refinement and/or amorphization at the surface. This modified microstructure rapidly forms and sustains a self-healing passive oxide film that acts as a continuous barrier, reducing both the electrochemical dissolution (corrosion) and the abrasive action of wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, samples that develop this adaptive surface layer will exhibit a lower friction coefficient, reduced wear volume, and lower corrosion current density during combined tribocorrosion tests. The synergy between mechanically induced nanostructuring and chemical passivation should result in measurable decreases in mass loss from both wear and corrosion components.
generation.baseline: A high-entropy alloy of similar composition and bulk microstructure that is processed without controlled pre-conditioning to promote adaptive nanostructuring.
generation.boundary: This prediction is expected to hold under conditions where the applied mechanical load is sufficient to induce surface nanostructuring without causing bulk failure, and in corrosive environments that allow passivation. In extremely aggressive environments (e.g., very high chloride concentration or very high loads causing oxide spallation), the protective mechanism might be overwhelmed.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative contribution of the microstructural nanostructuring versus inherent chemical passivation to the overall resistance is not yet fully defined, and the optimum alloy compositions and processing conditions to maximize this synergistic effect remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of HEA samples: one set engineered to promote surface nanostructuring (e.g., via a pre-conditioning sliding treatment or optimized processing parameters) and a control set without such treatment. Subject both sets to identical tribocorrosion testing in a 3.5 wt% NaCl solution at room temperature under a constant sliding load. Use in situ and post-test characterization (SEM/TEM and electrochemical measurements) to assess surface morphology evolution and passive film continuity.
measurements: Wear track profiling (to quantify wear volume and friction coefficient)
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) and potentiodynamic polarization (to determine corrosion rates)
High-resolution SEM/TEM imaging of the post-test surface to assess grain refinement/amorphization and passive film formation
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not exhibit a significantly refined (or partially amorphized) surface layer with a continuous, protective oxide film—and if their wear and corrosion metrics (e.g., friction coefficient, wear volume, corrosion current density) are not statistically lower than those of the control samples—then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractAlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy (HEA) films with strong amorphization were obtained by co-filter cathode vacuum arc deposition, and the effect of thermal shock on the films was investigated in order to explore the protection mechanism of HEA films against mechanical components in extreme service environments. The results show that after annealing at 800 °C for 1 h, the formation of a dense ZrTiO4 composite oxide layer on the surface actively prevents the oxidation from continuing, so that the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film exhibits excellent oxidation resistance at 800 °C in air. In the friction-corrosion coupling environment, the AlCrTiZrMo HEA film annealed at 800 °C for 1 h shows the best tribocorrosion resistance due to the stable dense microstructure and excellent mechanical properties, and its ΔOCP, COF and wear rate possess the smallest values of 0.055, 0.04 and 1.34 × 10−6 mm−3·N−1·m−1.Keywords: AlCrTiZrMo high-entropy alloy film, thermal shock, oxidation, tribocorrosion

To address the synergistic degradation mechanisms in engineering service environments, we propose a boron microalloying strategy to enhance the multifunctional surface performance of AlCoCrFeNiMo-based high-entropy alloys. AlCoCrFeNiMoTiBx coatings (x = 0, 0.5, 1, and 1.5) were fabricated on Q235 steel substrates using laser cladding. The microstructure of the coatings was characterized using scanning electron microscope (SEM) and energy dispersive spectrometer (EDS), while their wear and corrosion resistance were evaluated through tribological and electrochemical tests. The key findings indicate that boron addition preserves the original body-centered cubic (BCC) and σ phases in the coating while promoting the in situ formation of TiB2, leading to lattice distortion. With increasing B content, the BCC phase becomes refined, and both the fraction and size of TiB2 particles increase. Boron incorporation improves the coating’s microhardness and wear resistance, with the highest wear resistance achieved at x = 1, where abrasive and oxidative wear predominate. AbstractHigh-entropy alloys could provide a solution for corrosion resistance due to their impressive properties. Solid-state processing of high purity Co, Cr, Fe, Ni and Mo metallic powders and consolidation resulted in a bulk material that was further machined into electro spark deposition electrodes. After the stainless steel substrate surface preparation, thin successive layers of the high-entropy alloy were deposited and Pull-Off testing was performed on the newly obtained coating, for a better understanding of the adhesion efficiency of this technique. Good adhesion of the coating to the substrate was proved by the test and no cracks or exfoliations were present. Corrosion resistance testing was performed in a liquid solution of 3.5 wt.% NaCl for 6 h at room temperature and the results obtained validated our hypothesis that CoCrFeNiMo0.85 high-entropy alloys could provide corrosion resistance when coating a stainless steel substrate.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, mechanical alloying, coatings, adhesion
